questions.question: Who created the Python programming language?
questions.hint: Think about the Dutch programmer who began developing Python near the end of the 1980s.
questions.explanation: Python was created by Guido van Rossum, a Dutch programmer who began working on it in December 1989. Dennis Ritchie created C, James Gosling created Java, and Bjarne Stroustrup created C++.

questions.question: What is the origin of the name 'Python'?
options: It is named after a large snake species
It is an acronym formed from its core design goals
It is named after the British comedy series Monty Python's Flying Circus
It is named after a serpent from Greek mythology
questions.hint: Think about the creator's personal hobbies and interests at the time he chose the name, not the logo.
questions.explanation: Guido van Rossum was a fan of the comedy series Monty Python's Flying Circus and chose the name for that reason. Although the snake logo is widely used, the name does not come from the animal. It is also not an acronym.

questions.question: Which description best fits Python as a programming language?
options: A low-level, compiled language used only for system programming
A markup language used to design web pages
A purely functional language with no support for objects
A high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language
questions.hint: Consider how much Python hides hardware details, how its code gets executed, and how many kinds of tasks it is used for.
questions.explanation: Python is high-level because it abstracts away hardware details. It is interpreted because code is executed by an interpreter, after being compiled to bytecode internally. It is general-purpose because it is used for web development, automation, data science, AI and more. It supports procedural, object-oriented and functional styles.

questions.question: How does Python define blocks of code such as the body of a function or loop?
options: Semicolons at the end of each line
questions.hint: Picture a Python function next to the same function in C or Java, and notice what visually marks its body.
questions.explanation: Python uses indentation (leading whitespace) to mark code blocks. This is a distinctive design choice that enforces readable code. Curly braces are used in C, C++ and Java, and begin...end is used in Pascal-style languages.

questions.question: In which year was Python 3.0 (also called 'Python 3000') officially released?
questions.hint: Python 2.0 appeared in 2000, so think about how long it took before the next major version arrived.
questions.explanation: Python 3.0 was released in December 2008. Python 2.0 came out in 2000. Python 3 deliberately broke backward compatibility to fix design flaws in the language.

questions.question: Python's design was influenced by an earlier teaching language developed at CWI in the Netherlands. Which language was it?
questions.hint: Recall the language Guido worked on at the Dutch research institute before creating Python, and which of these was built mainly for teaching.
questions.explanation: Guido van Rossum worked on the ABC language at CWI (Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica). Python was conceived as a successor to ABC that could handle exceptions and interface with the Amoeba operating system. ABC's emphasis on readability and simplicity carried over into Python.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the result of the expression 7 / 2 in Python 2 versus Python 3?
questions.hint: Consider whether the / operator treated two integer operands the same way in both versions.
questions.explanation: In Python 2, the / operator performed integer (floor) division when both operands were integers, so 7 / 2 gave 3. In Python 3, / always performs true division and returns 3.5. Floor division in Python 3 requires the // operator.

questions.question: Which of the following is the reference (default) implementation of Python, written in the C language?
questions.hint: Think about which implementation you get when you download Python from python.org, and which platforms the others are tied to.
questions.explanation: CPython is the standard and most widely used implementation of Python, written in C. It compiles source code to bytecode and executes it on a virtual machine. Jython targets the Java Virtual Machine, IronPython targets .NET, and PyPy is an alternative implementation with a JIT compiler written in a restricted subset of Python.

questions.question: What happens when you run the statement `import this` in a Python interpreter?
options: It lists all built-in modules available in Python
It prints the Python license text
It displays the current Python version information
It prints 'The Zen of Python', a set of guiding principles for Python's design
questions.hint: This module is a well-known hidden Easter egg, so think about what a playful surprise from Python's community might show.
questions.explanation: The `this` module is a built-in Easter egg that prints 'The Zen of Python', written by Tim Peters and documented as PEP 20. It contains aphorisms such as 'Readability counts' and 'Simple is better than complex', which summarize Python's design philosophy.

questions.question: Which Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) is the official style guide for writing Python code?
questions.hint: Recall which PEP is followed when deciding how code should be formatted, including indentation, naming and line length.
questions.explanation: PEP 8 is the style guide for Python code. It covers indentation, naming conventions, line length and more. PEP 20 is the Zen of Python, PEP 257 covers docstring conventions, and PEP 484 introduced type hints.

questions.question: A developer runs the legacy Python 2 line `print "Hello, CodeVerse"` using a Python 3 interpreter. What is the result?
options: It prints Hello, CodeVerse along with a deprecation warning
It raises a NameError at runtime
questions.hint: Remember how print changed between versions, and think about whether Python rejects this line before or after starting to run it.
questions.explanation: In Python 2, print was a statement. In Python 3 it became a built-in function, so it must be called with parentheses: print("Hello, CodeVerse"). The old syntax is rejected when the code is parsed, so Python 3 raises a SyntaxError before any code runs.

questions.question: Guido van Rossum held the title 'Benevolent Dictator For Life' (BDFL) of Python for many years. Which statement correctly describes how Python is governed today?
options: He stepped down as BDFL in 2018, and since 2019 a five-member elected Steering Council has guided the language
He still holds the BDFL title and approves every language change personally
The Python Software Foundation's CEO appoints a new BDFL every five years
Python is now controlled by a single corporate owner who decides the roadmap
questions.hint: Think about how Python's leadership changed after the heated debate over assignment expressions in 2018.
questions.explanation: Guido announced in July 2018 that he was stepping down as BDFL following the heated discussion around PEP 572 (assignment expressions). The community adopted a new governance model (PEP 8016), and a five-member Steering Council, elected by core developers, has guided Python since 2019. The PSF supports the community but does not approve each language change, and no single company owns Python.

questions.question: Which of the following is a genuine difference between Python 3 and Python 2, rather than a feature shared by both?
options: Python 3 uses dynamic typing, while Python 2 used static typing
In Python 3, the str type holds Unicode text by default, whereas in Python 2 str held bytes
Python 3 uses indentation for blocks, while Python 2 used braces
questions.hint: First rule out features that both versions already shared, then think about how each version treats text versus binary data.
questions.explanation: One of the biggest changes in Python 3 was that str represents Unicode text and bytes is a separate type for binary data. In Python 2, str was a byte string and Unicode needed a separate unicode type. Dynamic typing, indentation-based blocks and reference counting were all present in both versions.

questions.question: Which option lists these Python milestones in the correct chronological order?
questions.hint: Compare the years given in each option and check whether any release appears before a version that came earlier.
questions.explanation: Guido began development in December 1989. The first public release, 0.9.0, came in February 1991, followed by Python 1.0 in January 1994 and Python 2.0 in October 2000. Python 3.0 arrived in December 2008. The version numbers match the release order, and every other option scrambles it.

questions.question: On what date did Python 2.7 officially reach its end of life, after which it received no further official support or security fixes?
questions.hint: The original retirement plan was postponed to give developers extra time to migrate, so think about when that extended period ended.
questions.explanation: Python 2.7 was originally planned to be retired in 2015, but the date was extended to give the community more time to migrate to Python 3. It officially reached end of life on January 1, 2020. A last release, 2.7.18, followed in April 2020. 2008 was the release year of Python 3.0, not the end of Python 2.
